lead: A practical source can be drawn as a voltage source with a series resistance or as a current source with a parallel resistance. Both give the same voltage and current at the terminals. A star of three resistors and a delta of three resistors are also two drawings of one three-terminal network. These two swaps turn awkward circuits into simple series-parallel circuits. You use them before mesh or node analysis, and inside Thevenin and Norton work. The arithmetic is small; the skill is choosing the right swap and keeping the source arrow correct.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for practical and ideal sources, and Chapter 1.4 for series-parallel reduction and dividers.

blocks.text: Every real source has some internal resistance. A 12 V battery with 0.5 Ω inside is not ideal. At the two terminals, a voltage source V_s in series with R and a current source I_s in parallel with the same R look identical if I_s = V_s ÷ R. That is the source transformation.

Open circuit: the voltage source gives V_s across the terminals; the current source gives I_s × R = V_s. Short circuit: the voltage source gives V_s ÷ R = I_s; the current source gives I_s. Same two tests, same terminal behaviour.

items: Identify a practical voltage source: value V_s volts, series resistance R ohms.
Draw current source I_s in parallel with the same R.
Point the arrow inside the current source from − to +, toward the terminal that acts as +. Current leaves that terminal into the outside circuit and returns to −.
Reverse: V_s = I_s × R, keep R in series, and put the positive terminal where the arrow leaves the source.

blocks.text: V_s = I_s R    and    I_s = V_s / R
blocks.where: V_s is the source voltage in volts; I_s is the source current in amperes; R is the internal resistance in ohms. The same R changes position, not value.

blocks.text: Only practical sources transform. An ideal voltage source has R = 0, so I_s would be infinite; no finite current source replaces it. An ideal current source has R = ∞, so V_s would be infinite; no finite voltage source replaces it. Use the swap to combine parallel current sources or series voltage sources, and to simplify a circuit before applying Chapter 1.4.

sections.h3: Star and delta at three terminals

blocks.text: Three resistors can meet at one node, a star, or form a closed triangle, a delta. A star has arms R_a, R_b, R_c from terminals a, b, c to the common node n. A delta has sides R_ab between a and b, R_bc between b and c, R_ca between c and a. At terminals a, b, c the two networks are equivalent when their resistance between every pair of terminals matches.

blocks.where: Delta to star. R_a, R_b, R_c are star arms in ohms at terminals a, b, c. R_ab, R_bc, R_ca are delta sides in ohms. The numerator uses the two delta sides touching terminal a. R_b and R_c follow by rotating the letters.

blocks.text: R_ab = (R_a R_b + R_b R_c + R_c R_a) / R_c
blocks.where: Star to delta. R_ab is the delta side between a and b in ohms; R_c is the star arm opposite side ab in ohms. R_bc uses R_a, and R_ca uses R_b.

blocks.text: Balanced case: all three star arms equal R_star, or all three delta sides equal R_delta. Then R_delta = 3 R_star, and R_star = R_delta ÷ 3. Never use both factors together.

items: Mark the three terminals a, b, c.
For delta to star, add the three sides, then divide the product of the two sides meeting at each terminal by that sum.
For star to delta, add the three pair products, then divide by the star arm opposite the side you want.
Use these when a bridge blocks series-parallel reduction; convert one star or delta, then apply Chapter 1.4.

spec.title: Two-way source transformation
spec.aria: Two blocks, a 12 volt source with a 6 ohm series resistance and a 2 ampere source with a 6 ohm parallel resistance, joined by arrows in both directions with the conversion formulas.

examples.question: A 12 V source in series with 6 Ω feeds a 3 Ω load. (a) Convert the source and find the load current from the converted circuit. (b) Convert a star of three 9 Ω resistors into its equivalent delta.
steps: Label V_s = 12 V, R = 6 Ω, load R_L = 3 Ω.
Converted current: I_s = V_s ÷ R = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. The 6 Ω stays in parallel with the 2 A source.
In the converted circuit, the 6 Ω source resistance is in parallel with the 3 Ω load: R_p = (6 × 3) ÷ (6 + 3) = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 Ω.
Current divider for the load: I_L = I_s × R ÷ (R + R_L) = 2 × 6 ÷ (6 + 3) = 1.333 A.
Check in the original series circuit: R_total = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 9 = 1.333 A. The two answers match.
Balanced star to delta: R_delta = 3 × R_star = 3 × 9 = 27 Ω on each side, so R_ab = R_bc = R_ca = 27 Ω.
examples.answer: The converted source is 2 A in parallel with 6 Ω; the load current is 1.333 A, matching the original 1.333 A; each side of the equivalent delta is 27 Ω.
examples.check:
V=12.0
R=6.0
RL=3.0
print(V/R)
print((R*RL)/(R+RL))
print((V/R)*(R/(R+RL)))
print(V/(R+RL))

traps: Reversing the current-source arrow. Inside the current source the arrow points from − to +, toward the source's + terminal. Current leaves that + terminal, flows through the outside circuit, and returns to −. The + terminal of the equivalent voltage source is the terminal the arrow points to.
Trying to transform an ideal source. R = 0 for an ideal voltage source and R = ∞ for an ideal current source leave no finite series or parallel resistor, so no partner source exists.
Using the series resistance as a parallel resistance, or the reverse. The same number R changes position, not value.
In star-delta work, dividing by the wrong arm. For R_ab use the star arm opposite side ab, which is R_c; for R_a use the product of the two delta sides touching node a.
Mixing the balanced factors: R_delta = 3 R_star, but R_star = R_delta ÷ 3. A factor-of-3 error is common.

quiz.q: State the two source transformation formulas.
quiz.a: V_s = I_s R and I_s = V_s ÷ R. The resistance R is in series with the voltage source and in parallel with the current source.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal voltage source have no current-source partner?
quiz.a: An ideal voltage source has R = 0. The conversion would need I_s = V_s ÷ 0, which is infinite. No finite current source can replace it.

quiz.q: A 24 V source has 8 Ω in series. Find its current-source equivalent.
quiz.a: I_s = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 A. The equivalent is a 3 A source in parallel with 8 Ω, with the arrow pointing the way the 24 V source drove current through the outside circuit.

quiz.q: A delta has R_ab = 6 Ω, R_bc = 12 Ω, R_ca = 18 Ω. Find the star arms.
A 5 A current source has 4 Ω in parallel. What voltage source replaces it, and where is the positive terminal?
quiz.a: V_s = 5 × 4 = 20 V in series with 4 Ω. The positive terminal is where the arrow leaves the source when it delivers current to the outside circuit.

quiz.q: A bridge has a balanced star of 4 Ω arms. What delta replaces it, and when would you use a star-to-delta conversion?
quiz.a: R_delta = 3 × 4 = 12 Ω on each side. In most bridges the useful direction is delta to star: replacing the delta by a star removes the loop and leaves plain series-parallel branches. A star-to-delta is used only when the new delta sides land in parallel with existing branches.

quiz.q: In the worked example, a student converts 12 V and 6 Ω to 2 A and 6 Ω, then puts the 6 Ω in series with the 3 Ω load and says the load current is 2 A. Explain the error and give the correct value.
quiz.a: The conversion puts the 6 Ω in parallel with the source, and the load is also in parallel, not in series. The correct load current is 2 × 6 ÷ (6 + 3) = 1.333 A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators keep Norton-equivalent models at nodes, and the same maths appears in delta-wye motor starters. Power engineers use per-phase star-delta conversion for transformer banks and three-phase loads, which you will meet in Unit 2. In AC, resistors become impedances and the formulas still hold with complex Z. Search next for 'Norton equivalent', 'delta-wye conversion' and 'star-delta starter'.
